edited_rows.rationale: The title’s historical note — “For the Chief Musician. By David the servant of Yahweh, who spoke to Yahweh the words of this song in the day that Yahweh delivered him from the hand of all his enemies, and from the hand of Saul” (web:Ps.18.0) — opens with לַמְנַצֵּ֤חַ (“For the Chief Musician.”), the phrase לְעֶ֥בֶד יְהוָ֗ה, “servant of Yahweh,” following as words 2-3, and closes with שָׁאֽוּל, “and from the hand of Saul” (oshb:Ps.18.1); the staged extract splits it into 20 whitespace-separated tokens, naming Chief-Musician dedication, Davidic authorship, servant status, compositional occasion, and the Saul/enemies deliverance setting that the psalm’s own rescue narrative retells. The declarative epithet list “I love you, Yahweh, my strength” through “my shield, and the horn of my salvation, my high tower” (web:Ps.18.1-Ps.18.2) states the psalmist’s confidence in Yahweh before the narrative proper begins; “The cords of death surrounded me” (web:Ps.18.4) shifts to finite narrative describing the crisis, and the strophe closes on the cry being answered — “He heard my voice out of his temple. My cry before him came into his ears” (web:Ps.18.6) — which sets up the theophany as Yahweh’s response.
edited_rows.rejected_alternative: Splitting the epithet list (web:Ps.18.1-Ps.18.2) from the distress narrative that follows would separate a static confidence-confession from the crisis-and-cry it is answering.

He routed them with great lightning bolts.” web:Ps.18.14) — that culminates in direct address returning at its close, “at your rebuke, Yahweh” (web:Ps.18.15), where the psalmist speaks to Yahweh directly — the 2ms-suffixed מִגַּעֲרָ֣תְךָ֣ (“your rebuke”) and אַפֶּֽךָ (“your nostrils”), oshb:Ps.18.16, address Yahweh mid-clause — pivoting the theophany's cosmic disclosure back into the psalmist's own address to God, preparing the rescue narrative in the psalmist's own voice that opens the next strophe.
edited_rows.rejected_alternative: Folding this storm-cloud disclosure into the preceding descent strophe would obscure the return to direct address that marks this movement's own close.

He drew me out of many waters” (web:Ps.18.16) answers the theophany with the rescue it accomplishes, told now in a chain of finite verbs (sent, took, drew, delivered, brought out); the waters lexeme of the theophany’s own flood imagery carries across the seam into this opening verse (מִמַּ֥יִם, oshb:Ps.18.17, echoing אֲפִ֥יקֵי מַ֗יִם at oshb:Ps.18.16 = web:Ps.18.15) even as the theophany’s storm/fire/descent imagery itself does not continue; the movement closes on cause rather than event — “He delivered me, because he delighted in me” (web:Ps.18.19) — before the strophe that follows turns from narrated rescue to the psalmist’s own righteousness.

edited_rows.rationale: The rhetorical question “For who is God, except Yahweh? Who is a rock, besides our God, the God who arms me with strength, and makes my way perfect?” (web:Ps.18.31-Ps.18.32) reopens the psalm’s own rock-epithet from web:Ps.18.2 in interrogative form; its closing clause, “the God who arms me with strength, and makes my way perfect” (הָ֭אֵל...תָּמִ֣ים דַּרְכִּֽי, oshb:Ps.18.33 = web:Ps.18.32), repeats the designation-and-integrity phrase that closed the preceding strophe, “As for God, his way is perfect” (הָאֵל֮...תָּמִ֪ים דַּ֫רְכּ֥וֹ, oshb:Ps.18.31 = web:Ps.18.30) — a frame whose two occurrences straddle this row’s own opening seam, disclosed rather than treated as unique to either row. The strophe then turns to the equipping proper: feet like a deer’s (web:Ps.18.33), hands taught to war (“teaches my hands to war,” oshb:Ps.18.35 word 3 לַמִּלְחָמָ֑ה = web:Ps.18.34), the shield and right hand of web:Ps.18.35, closing “You have enlarged my steps under me, My feet have not slipped” (web:Ps.18.36). The battle-phrase collocation of web:Ps.18.34 recurs byte-identically at web:Ps.18.39 (“armed me with strength to the battle.” לַמִּלְחָמָ֑ה, oshb:Ps.18.40 word 3), so the equipping vocabulary itself continues past this row’s own close, disclosed as a second cross-seam continuity; the shift this row marks is from second-person divine-gift description to combat verbs opening in the psalmist’s own first-person voice at the strophe that follows (“I will pursue my enemies, and overtake them.” web:Ps.18.37).
edited_rows.rejected_alternative: Extending this strophe into the victory narrative that follows would merge Yahweh's equipping gifts with the psalmist's own combat actions that those gifts enable.

edited_rows.rationale: The title “For the Chief Musician. A Psalm by David” (web:Ps.19.0) opens a psalm whose two halves name God differently. “The heavens declare the glory of God” (web:Ps.19.1) renders אֵ֑ל, El (oshb:Ps.19.2) — the pointed divine name, distinct from the negative particle אַֽל, 'not,' that appears later in this psalm at oshb:Ps.19.14 — and the covenant name Yahweh does not occur within web:Ps.19.1-Ps.19.6 (0 occurrences across 6 verses, confirmed by direct verse-text inspection against the whole-psalm Yahweh count in the device inventory, not a sweep.py lexeme-index feature). This heavens-panel describes creation's speechless testimony through the sun's circuit — “There is no speech nor language where their voice is not heard” (web:Ps.19.3), “His going out is from the end of the heavens, his circuit to its ends” (web:Ps.19.6) — in third-person cosmic description without addressing God directly; the panel that follows opens by naming Yahweh's law and shifts into the psalmist's own petitionary voice, marking the seam between the psalm's two halves.
edited_rows.rejected_alternative: Treating Psalm 19 as one undivided strophe would fold this speechless cosmic testimony together with the psalmist's own petitionary voice that opens in the panel that follows.

edited_rows.rationale: The opening strophe is second-person intercession addressed to Yahweh on the king’s behalf, opening “May Yahweh answer you in the day of trouble” (web:Ps.20.1) and running through a chain of jussive petitions (help, support, remembered offerings) that closes on the Selah-marked “remember all your offerings, and accept your burned sacrifice. Selah.” (web:Ps.20.3). The jussive register continues through web:Ps.20.4 (“May he grant you your heart's desire,” יִֽתֶּן, oshb:Ps.20.5), and the verb mood shifts from jussive petition to cohortative communal vow only at this row's own closing verse, “We will triumph in your salvation... we will set up our banners” (web:Ps.20.5, נְרַנְּנָ֤ה/נִדְגֹּ֑ל, oshb:Ps.20.6), which the strophe that follows carries forward as a confident declaration on the king's behalf.
edited_rows.rejected_alternative: One whole-psalm row was considered given the psalm’s 9-verse length, but the jussive-petition block (1-5) and the declarative confidence block (6-9, opening “Now I know”, web:Ps.20.6) are distinct enough in mood and person to warrant separate rows.

Let him deliver him. Let him rescue him, since he delights in him.” (web:Ps.22.8), a self-contained reported speech that seals the unit.
edited_rows.rejected_alternative: Extending this strophe through web:Ps.22.11 (folding in the birth-trust return) was considered, but the direct second-person address to God that resumes at web:Ps.22.9 marks a clean addressee return distinct from this description-mode unit.
observed_substrate_signals: WEB sets off the taunt with quotation marks (web:Ps.22.8), a single-witness translation convention; the MT itself carries no speech-introducing verb at this seam (oshb:Ps.22.9 = web:Ps.22.8 opens asyndetically)
no 1st- or 2nd-person address to God within web:Ps.22.6-Ps.22.8
edited_rows.device_notes: The mockers’ taunt is set off by WEB’s quotation marks (a single-witness, tier-4 translation convention); the MT carries no speech-introducing verb or other formal marking device at this seam — oshb:Ps.22.9 (= web:Ps.22.8) opens asyndetically with the imperative גֹּ֣ל, confirmed clean of second-person address to God across web:Ps.22.6-Ps.22.8.

edited_rows.rationale: The strophe returns to second-person address to God with the birth-trust motif, “But you brought me out of the womb. You made me trust while at my mother’s breasts” (web:Ps.22.9), “I was thrown on you from my mother’s womb” (web:Ps.22.10), and closes the plea “Don’t be far from me, for trouble is near. For there is no one to help” (web:Ps.22.11), which hinges the psalm into the pure description that follows.
edited_rows.rejected_alternative: Merging this strophe with the following enemy-imagery block (9-18) was considered; explicit you/your address recedes once the third-person bulls/lions imagery opens at web:Ps.22.12, though an embedded second-person verb-suffix recurs once more at web:Ps.22.15 (תִּשְׁפְּתֵֽנִי, 'you lay me,' oshb:Ps.22.16) before the catalog resumes uninterrupted third-person description; this row's own seam still marks the point where free-standing you/your address gives way to sustained third-person imagery.
observed_substrate_signals: second-person address to God (“you”, “your”) present in 2 of 3 verses across web:Ps.22.9-Ps.22.11 (web:Ps.22.9, web:Ps.22.10); web:Ps.22.11 carries no free-standing you/your token, though its verb (תִּרְחַ֣ק, oshb:Ps.22.12) continues address to God without an independent pronoun or suffix
edited_rows.device_notes: The birth-trust motif closes the psalm’s opening address cycle before its central affliction catalog opens.

edited_rows.rationale: The strophe is the extended affliction catalog in the third person, opening “Many bulls have surrounded me. Strong bulls of Bashan have encircled me” (web:Ps.22.12), through lions (13), the pouring-out and melting imagery (14-15), the encircling dogs and pierced hands and feet (16), the counted bones (17), and closing “They divide my garments among them. They cast lots for my clothing” (web:Ps.22.18), with third-person description dominant throughout except a single embedded second-person verb-suffix at web:Ps.22.15 (תִּשְׁפְּתֵֽנִי, 'you lay me,' oshb:Ps.22.16), a brief address to God without a free pronoun before the catalog's third-person mode resumes.
edited_rows.rejected_alternative: Splitting the catalog at the animal-imagery/bodily-imagery seam (web:Ps.22.14) was considered, but the images run as one largely unbroken description — interrupted only by the embedded second-person verb-suffix at web:Ps.22.15 (תִּשְׁפְּתֵֽנִי, oshb:Ps.22.16) — with no other address shift or formal marker inside the span to argue a sub-boundary.
observed_substrate_signals: poetry_lines: 3 at Ps.22.14, 2 at Ps.22.15 and Ps.22.16 (verse_map_web), the psalm’s peak per-verse counts
WEB carries a footnote at web:Ps.22.16 on a Dead Sea Scrolls/Masoretic reading difference; the footnote is tier-4 and not used as boundary evidence
edited_rows.device_notes: The third-person affliction catalog forms Psalm 22's 7-verse strophe, sustained in one descriptive mode throughout except one embedded second-person verb-suffix (web:Ps.22.15 = oshb:Ps.22.16).

edited_rows.rationale: The strophe reopens direct address to God, “But don’t be far off, Yahweh. You are my help. Hurry to help me!” (web:Ps.22.19), whose Hebrew opens “וְאַתָּ֣ה יְ֭הוָה” (oshb:Ps.22.20), echoing the same contrastive formula that opened the turn at web:Ps.22.3, then closes the plea “Save me from the lion’s mouth! Yes, you have rescued me from the horns of the wild oxen” (web:Ps.22.21), where the verb shifts from imperative plea to a completed-action claim.
edited_rows.rejected_alternative: Extending this strophe through web:Ps.22.22 (the vow-of-praise pivot) was considered, but web:Ps.22.22 opens a cohortative 1st-person vow (“I will declare”) distinct from the imperative plea register of 19-21.
observed_substrate_signals: consonantal-SKELETON SUBSTRING sweep of וְאַתָּ֥ה: 23 hits book-wide (22 as the free-standing pronoun+conjunction formula, plus 1 prefix-substring collision inside a longer word, e.g. oshb:Ps.119.45's בָרְחָבָ֑ה, sharing the same four-consonant run); exactly 2 of the free-standing occurrences fall inside Psalm 22 (oshb:Ps.22.4 and oshb:Ps.22.20), one at each renewed address
edited_rows.device_notes: The repeated contrastive-address formula corroborates two internal turns in Psalm 22 without driving either boundary alone.

edited_rows.rationale: This strophe opens on the celebrated lament-to-praise pivot, “I will declare your name to my brothers. Among the assembly, I will praise you.” (web:Ps.22.22), a cohortative vow answering the plea just closed, then moves into the call for the assembly’s praise (23), a reflection on God’s attention to the afflicted (24), and vows paid “in the great assembly” (25), closing “The humble shall eat and be satisfied… Let your hearts live forever” (web:Ps.22.26).
edited_rows.rejected_alternative: Attaching web:Ps.22.22 to the preceding plea (19-22) as its resolution was the rival reading and cannot be excluded on the bytes alone; this row instead opens the vow-of-praise unit with it, since its opening cohortative, “I will declare” (אֲסַפְּרָ֣ה, oshb:Ps.22.23), together with the paired verb “I will praise” (אֲהַלְלֶֽךָּ, oshb:Ps.22.23, a 1cs form without the cohortative's paragogic he, its object suffix blocking the marker) match the register of the assembly-facing verses that follow rather than the imperative plea register before it.
observed_substrate_signals: verb mood shift: imperative (“Save me” web:Ps.22.21) to cohortative (“I will declare” web:Ps.22.22)
no selah anywhere in Psalm 22 (pmarks_Ps.json)
edited_rows.device_notes: The lament-to-praise pivot at web:Ps.22.22 is a contested seam in Psalm 22’s structure; this row registers the boundary at medium confidence rather than overstating it.

edited_rows.rationale: The closing strophe widens scope from the assembly to the whole earth, “All the ends of the earth shall remember and turn to Yahweh. All the relatives of the nations shall worship before you.” (web:Ps.22.27), through universal worship (28-29) and posterity “that shall be born” (web:Ps.22.31), a scope expansion distinct from the Israel/assembly-facing vocabulary (‘my brothers’, ‘the great assembly’) of the preceding strophe.
edited_rows.rejected_alternative: Folding these verses into the preceding vow-of-praise strophe (22-31 as one unit) was considered, but the shift from assembly-scoped vocabulary to “All the ends of the earth” (web:Ps.22.27) marks a real expansion of addressee scope.
observed_substrate_signals: lexical scope shift: “the great assembly” (web:Ps.22.25) to “All the ends of the earth” (web:Ps.22.27)
edited_rows.device_notes: Psalm 22 closes on a universal horizon that completes its shared parent arc from the opening cry.

edited_rows.rationale: Psalm 23 is one unbroken shepherd movement, opening “Yahweh is my shepherd; I shall lack nothing.” (web:Ps.23.1), through pastures and still waters (2), restored paths (3), the valley of the shadow of death (4), the table before enemies (5), and closing “I will dwell in Yahweh’s house forever” (web:Ps.23.6); at 6 verses it falls under the book’s short-psalm threshold for a single row, and the title sits inside MT verse 1 rather than as a separately counted verse.
edited_rows.rejected_alternative: A two-strophe split at web:Ps.23.3/Ps.23.4 (following the shift from third-person description of the shepherd to second-person address, “for you are with me”) was considered, but rejected as unnecessary fragmentation of a psalm short enough for one row: it carries no refrain, no vocative opener, and no selah to mark a formal internal seam.
observed_substrate_signals: person shift: third person (web:Ps.23.1-Ps.23.3) to second person (“you are with me” web:Ps.23.4) is texture, not a formal marker
psalm length 6 verses, within the owner-ruled whole_psalm threshold
edited_rows.device_notes: Psalm 23 is complete in itself as one composition, its parent grouping simply Psalm 23.

edited_rows.rationale: The closing strophe is the antiphonal gate dialogue, opening “Lift up your heads, you gates! Be lifted up, you everlasting doors, and the King of glory will come in.” (web:Ps.24.7), Hebrew “שְׂא֤וּ שְׁעָרִ֨ים רָֽאשֵׁיכֶ֗ם…” (oshb:Ps.24.7), answered “Who is the King of glory?” (8), whose opening 3-word formula repeats identically (sweep: 2 verses book-wide) at web:Ps.24.9, Hebrew “שְׂא֤וּ שְׁעָרִ֨ים רָֽאשֵׁיכֶ֗ם” (oshb:Ps.24.9) matching oshb:Ps.24.7’s own opening exactly, though the two full verses differ in 2 of 9 words elsewhere (niphal/qal at word 4, plene/defective spelling at word 7), and closes “Who is this King of glory? Yahweh of Armies is the King of glory! Selah.” (web:Ps.24.10). The strophe opens just after the Selah that marked the close of the preceding entrance-liturgy unit at Ps 24:6.
edited_rows.rejected_alternative: Splitting the two question-answer exchanges (7-8 and 9-10) into separate rows was considered, but the identical 3-word gate-command opening (sweep: 2 verses book-wide) that both exchanges share argues for one antiphonal unit rather than two, even though the two full verses differ in 2 of 9 words beyond that opening formula.
observed_substrate_signals: web_selah: true at Ps.24.10 (pmarks_Ps.json selah key Ps.24.10 MT); the front-seam verse Ps.24.6 also carries selah (pmarks_Ps.json selah key Ps.24.6 MT)
consonantal sweep of the gate-command opening string: 2 verses book-wide, both inside this span (oshb:Ps.24.7, oshb:Ps.24.9)
consonantal sweep of ‘king of glory’: 4 verses / 5 occurrences book-wide, all inside this span (oshb:Ps.24.7-Ps.24.10)
edited_rows.device_notes: The gate liturgy’s antiphonal question-answer pattern is the psalm’s closing movement, gathered under its shared parent unit.

edited_rows.rationale: Ps.25.1 opens the psalm's address to Yahweh, “To you, Yahweh, I lift up my soul.” (web:Ps.25.1), and an imperative petition cluster carries through v. 7 — “Show me your ways, Yahweh. Teach me your paths.” (web:Ps.25.4), “Don't remember the sins of my youth, nor my transgressions. Remember me according to your loving kindness, for your goodness' sake, Yahweh.” (web:Ps.25.7). At v. 8 the register shifts to gnomic description of Yahweh's own character, “Good and upright is Yahweh, therefore he will instruct sinners in the way.” (web:Ps.25.8), continuing to the covenant-friendship saying of v. 14, “The friendship of Yahweh is with those who fear him. He will show them his covenant.” (web:Ps.25.14); a direct-address petition already recurs within this same span at v. 11, “For your name’s sake, Yahweh, pardon my iniquity, for it is great.” (web:Ps.25.11 = oshb:Ps.25.11, שִׁמְךָ֥ יְהוָ֑ה וְֽסָלַחְתָּ֥, ‘your name, Yahweh, and you have pardoned’), so the vv. 8-14 block is not pure third-person description but a gnomic frame interrupted once by direct petition, before petition resumes as the block’s sustained register at v. 15.
edited_rows.rejected_alternative: Treating Ps 25 as one continuous row is also defensible, since the acrostic sequence (with its two documented irregularities — the buried bet at v. 2 and the skipped waw at v. 6) still runs across the whole psalm without a break in verse-per-letter sequencing at the seam this row proposes.
observed_substrate_signals: imperative petition-verb cluster (show/teach/guide/remember) runs vv. 4-7
verse-initial gnomic shift at v. 8 opens third-person description of Yahweh's dealings
the covenant-friendship saying at v. 14 closes the didactic unit before petition resumes
edited_rows.device_notes: Rows of Psalm 25 group to one parent unit. The acrostic is irregular (psalm_device_inventory.json): the aleph word is v. 1's second word, אֵלֶ֥יךָ (oshb:Ps.25.1), the title לְדָוִ֡ד occupying word 1; the expected second letter bet does not open v. 2 — its opening word is אֱֽלֹהַ֗י (aleph again), with בְּךָ֣ (bet) surfacing as the second word (oshb:Ps.25.2); the expected sixth letter waw is skipped — v. 6 opens with the seventh letter zayin in זְכֹר (oshb:Ps.25.6).

edited_rows.rationale: V. 1 opens with a double petition for testing, “Judge me, Yahweh, for I have walked in my integrity. I have trusted also in Yahweh without wavering.” (web:Ps.26.1), “Examine me, Yahweh, and prove me. Try my heart and my mind.” (web:Ps.26.2), grounding the plea in a negative confession of avoiding the wicked — “I have not sat with deceitful men, neither will I go in with hypocrites.” (web:Ps.26.4), “I hate the assembly of evildoers, and will not sit with the wicked.” (web:Ps.26.5) — and a ritual-purity action, “I will wash my hands in innocence, so I will go about your altar, Yahweh,” (web:Ps.26.6), whose purpose clause continues directly into v. 7's thanksgiving. V. 8 opens a fresh declaration with a verse-initial vocative, “Yahweh, I love the habitation of your house, the place where your glory dwells.” (web:Ps.26.8), marking the next unit's start.
edited_rows.rejected_alternative: A boundary at v. 6 rather than v. 7 is possible, since v. 7's purpose clause continues v. 6's ritual action rather than opening new content.
observed_substrate_signals: double petition-verb cluster (judge/examine/prove) opens vv. 1-2
the ritual-purity action of v. 6 closes with a purpose clause naming thanksgiving before the vocative pivot at v. 8
edited_rows.device_notes: Under one parent unit, Psalm 26 gathers the rows here. V. 1's integrity clause sits medial (words 6-7 of 11), בְּתֻמִּ֣י הָלַ֑כְתִּי (oshb:Ps.26.1), 'I have walked in my integrity.' V. 11's integrity clause is also medial (words 2-3 of 5, followed by פְּדֵ֣נִי וְחָנֵּֽנִי), בְּתֻמִּ֥י אֵלֵ֗ךְ (oshb:Ps.26.11), 'I will walk in my integrity' — only the noun בְּתֻמִּ֣י/בְּתֻמִּ֥י recurs (byte-unequal, matching from accent_stripped tier down); the verbs (qatal הָלַ֑כְתִּי vs yiqtol אֵלֵ֗ךְ) differ at every tier. A shared-word echo bracketing the psalm, not a repeated phrase at its edges.

edited_rows.rationale: V. 8's vocative declaration, “Yahweh, I love the habitation of your house, the place where your glory dwells.” (web:Ps.26.8), opens a love-and-devotion unit that turns to a negative petition echoing vv. 4-5's dissociation from evildoers — “Don't gather my soul with sinners, nor my life with bloodthirsty men” (web:Ps.26.9) — before closing with the psalm's vow of integrity restated, “But as for me, I will walk in my integrity. Redeem me, and be merciful to me.” (web:Ps.26.11), resolving into the congregational blessing of v. 12.
edited_rows.rejected_alternative: A boundary at v. 9 rather than v. 8 is possible, since v. 8's vocative could be read as concluding the ritual unit rather than opening a new one.
observed_substrate_signals: verse-initial vocative Yahweh opens v. 8 (oshb:Ps.26.8), a clean address-shift marker
vv. 4-5's dissociation from evildoers recurs as negative petition in v. 9, and the opening integrity-vow language recurs in v. 11, bracketing the whole psalm
edited_rows.device_notes: V. 12 closes in a congregational setting, בְמִישׁ֑וֹר בְּ֝מַקְהֵלִ֗ים אֲבָרֵ֥ךְ יְהוָֽה (oshb:Ps.26.12; 'in an even place, in the congregations, I will bless Yahweh', web:Ps.26.12), moving the integrity vow into public praise.

edited_rows.rationale: The psalm opens in declarative confidence, “Yahweh is my light and my salvation. Whom shall I fear? Yahweh is the strength of my life. Of whom shall I be afraid?” (web:Ps.27.1), reporting rather than directly petitioning Yahweh through v. 6's resolution, “Now my head will be lifted up above my enemies around me. I will offer sacrifices of joy in his tent. I will sing, yes, I will sing praises to Yahweh.” (web:Ps.27.6). The mode changes sharply at v. 7, where the psalm turns to direct imperative address, “Hear, Yahweh, when I cry with my voice. Have mercy also on me, and answer me.” (web:Ps.27.7).
edited_rows.rejected_alternative: Reading vv. 1-14 as one integrated composition is also arguable, since the salvation-root noun opening v. 1 (וְ֭יִשְׁעִי, oshb:Ps.27.1) recurs across the seam at v. 9 (יִשְׁעִֽי, oshb:Ps.27.9), a shared root the declarative and petitionary halves both carry.
observed_substrate_signals: declarative confidence mode (report about Yahweh) runs vv. 1-6 with no imperative petition verb
v. 7 opens with the imperative שְׁמַע (“hear”) plus vocative Yahweh, marking the mode shift (oshb:Ps.27.7)
edited_rows.device_notes: Psalm 27 supplies the parent for its strophes.

edited_rows.rationale: V. 7 turns from the declarative confidence of the preceding verses to direct imperative petition, “Hear, Yahweh, when I cry with my voice. Have mercy also on me, and answer me.” (web:Ps.27.7), continuing through appeals against abandonment, “Don't hide your face from me. Don't put your servant away in anger. You have been my help. Don't abandon me, neither forsake me, God of my salvation.” (web:Ps.27.9), and closing with a doubled exhortation, “Wait for Yahweh. Be strong, and let your heart take courage. Yes, wait for Yahweh.” (web:Ps.27.14), that brackets the unit as its own close.
edited_rows.rejected_alternative: A boundary at v. 8 rather than v. 7 is possible, since v. 7's imperative could be read as closing the confidence report rather than opening the petition.
observed_substrate_signals: imperative-plus-vocative opening at v. 7 (שְׁמַע יְהוָ֖ה, oshb:Ps.27.7) shifts the address mode from report to direct petition — WEB's “Hear, Yahweh” (web:Ps.27.7)
the doubled exhortation “wait for Yahweh” (web:Ps.27.14) brackets the unit's own close
edited_rows.device_notes: The closing doubled exhortation at v. 14 functions as this row's own resolution.

edited_rows.rationale: The psalm opens with petition for a favorable divine answer, “To you, Yahweh, I call. My rock, don't be deaf to me, lest, if you are silent to me, I would become like those who go down into the pit.” (web:Ps.28.1), “Hear the voice of my petitions, when I cry to you, when I lift up my hands toward your Most Holy Place.” (web:Ps.28.2), then turns to an imprecation against the wicked, “Don't draw me away with the wicked, with the workers of iniquity who speak peace with their neighbors, but mischief is in their hearts.” (web:Ps.28.3), “Give them according to their work, and according to the wickedness of their doings. Give them according to the operation of their hands. Bring back on them what they deserve.” (web:Ps.28.4), closing with the reason for their judgment, “Because they don't respect the works of Yahweh, nor the operation of his hands, he will break them down and not build them up.” (web:Ps.28.5). V. 6 shifts abruptly to a declaration of answered prayer, “Blessed be Yahweh, because he has heard the voice of my petitions.” (web:Ps.28.6).
edited_rows.rejected_alternative: A boundary at v. 4 rather than v. 5 is possible, since v. 5's stated reason for judgment could be grouped with the imprecation that precedes it rather than closing it.
observed_substrate_signals: petition-verb cluster (call/hear/draw away) frames vv. 1-3

the Qal imperative for “give” occurs twice in v. 4 as two differing pointed forms of the same lemma — תֶּן (word 1) and תֵּ֣ן (word 8), oshb:Ps.28.4 — before a third imperative, הָשֵׁ֖ב (“repay”), closes the verse (oshb:Ps.28.4)
edited_rows.device_notes: Psalm 28's rows share one parent, the psalm itself.

edited_rows.rationale: V. 6 pivots the psalm from petition to praise with a doxological formula, “Blessed be Yahweh, because he has heard the voice of my petitions.” (web:Ps.28.6), and the declaration of trust continues through v. 7, “Yahweh is my strength and my shield. My heart has trusted in him, and I am helped. Therefore my heart greatly rejoices. With my song I will thank him.” (web:Ps.28.7), in third-person report that widens to Yahweh's own anointed at v. 8, “Yahweh is their strength. He is a stronghold of salvation to his anointed.” (web:Ps.28.8 = oshb:Ps.28.8, the 3ms suffix on “his anointed” מְשִׁיח֣וֹ, taking Yahweh — not the king — as antecedent), before direct second-person address to Yahweh opens the closing petition, “Save your people, and bless your inheritance. Be their shepherd also, and bear them up forever.” (web:Ps.28.9).
edited_rows.rejected_alternative: A boundary at v. 7 rather than v. 6 is possible, since v. 6's brief declaration could be read as closing the petition unit rather than opening the praise unit.
observed_substrate_signals: the doxological formula בָּר֥וּךְ יְהוָ֑ה (oshb:Ps.28.6) opens v. 6 as WEB's “Blessed be Yahweh” (web:Ps.28.6), marking the petition-to-praise pivot

third-person report runs through v. 8 (the anointed one's possessor is Yahweh, not the king: “his anointed” web:Ps.28.8 = oshb:Ps.28.8, 3ms suffix מְשִׁיח֣וֹ); direct second-person address to Yahweh begins only at v. 9, “your people... your inheritance” (web:Ps.28.9), a referent-widening scope shift, not an addressee shift, closing the psalm
edited_rows.device_notes: The בָּר֥וּךְ יְהוָ֑ה formula in v. 6 marks an internal petition-to-praise pivot, not one of the book's four boundary doxologies (oshb:Ps.28.6).

edited_rows.rationale: The psalm opens with a heavenly summons distinct from the storm theophany that follows: “Ascribe to Yahweh, you sons of the mighty, ascribe to Yahweh glory and strength.” (web:Ps.29.1), “Ascribe to Yahweh the glory due to his name. Worship Yahweh in holy array.” (web:Ps.29.2). The vocative addressee is “you sons of the mighty” (בְּנֵ֣י אֵלִ֑ים, oshb:Ps.29.1); Yahweh (לַֽ֭יהוָה) is the imperative's dative recipient, not its addressee. Vocative address stops after v. 2 rather than shifting to a different addressee — the storm's forces described from v. 3 onward (cedars, wilderness, deer) are third-person subjects, not addressees.
edited_rows.rejected_alternative: Grouping vv. 1-2 with the storm hymn as one unbroken invocation is also defensible, since both share the same imperative-vocative register; this candidate isolates the heavenly summons on its distinct addressee alone.
observed_substrate_signals: the imperative lemma “ascribe/give” (הבו) occurs 3 times across these 2 verses (oshb:Ps.29.1 words 3 and 7, oshb:Ps.29.2 word 1); the exact pointed spelling הָב֣וּ occurs 2 of those 3 times (oshb:Ps.29.1 word 3 and oshb:Ps.29.2 word 1), oshb:Ps.29.1 word 7 pointed differently as הָב֥וּ

the WEB phrase “sons of the mighty” (web:Ps.29.1) renders the vocative בְּנֵ֣י אֵלִ֑ים (oshb:Ps.29.1 words 5-6), this psalm's only named addressee; Yahweh, named as the imperative's dative recipient in vv. 1-2, is not himself addressed, and 0 vocative or second-person forms recur across oshb:Ps.29.3-Ps.29.9
edited_rows.device_notes: Psalm 29 forms one composition; its rows answer to one parent.

edited_rows.rationale: The refrain drops after v. 9, and the psalm closes with an enthronement declaration, “Yahweh sat enthroned at the Flood. Yes, Yahweh sits as King forever.” (web:Ps.29.10), resolving into a blessing on Yahweh's people, “Yahweh will give strength to his people. Yahweh will bless his people with peace.” (web:Ps.29.11), a scope shift from the storm's cosmic reach to the covenant community.
edited_rows.rejected_alternative: Keeping v. 10 inside the refrain unit is possible, since its enthronement language continues the theophany's storm imagery in form; this candidate isolates it with v. 11 on shared king/peace vocabulary that closes the psalm.
observed_substrate_signals: the refrain's final appearance is v. 9; v. 10 opens without the voice-of-Yahweh phrase, marking the drop (oshb:Ps.29.9, oshb:Ps.29.10)
